topics.chapterTitle: Protecting Shared Data with Mutexes and Locks
topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: When operations share mutable state, correctness depends on protecting the entire invariant rather than only individual assignments. A transfer between two accounts must preserve the total while preventing negative balances. This chapter uses RAII locks and multi-mutex acquisition to make that transaction visible, then separates deadlock avoidance for one operation from the wider lock-order discipline of an application.

Protecting individual variables is not the same as protecting the invariant of a multi-object operation.

blocks.text: The chapter uses a bounded transfer model to connect locks to invariants. It does not model a banking system’s durability, authorization, or distributed transactions. Its purpose is narrower and testable: make a two-account update indivisible with respect to the program’s cooperating threads, reject invalid operations without changing balances, and acquire the required locks without creating an avoidable circular wait.

topics.title: 17.1.1 Protecting Critical Sections
topics.summary: A mutex allows one thread at a time to hold a protected critical section. Every access participating in the same shared invariant must follow the chosen synchronization policy. Protecting writes but reading the same ordinary state without synchronization can still create a data race. A mutex member does not enforce correct use by itself.

blocks.text: A critical section is the region in which shared state is accessed under a synchronization discipline. The mutex is meaningful only if every conflicting access follows that discipline. blocks.text: Start with the invariant rather than the member layout. For a transfer, each balance must remain within its permitted range and a successful operation preserves the combined total. Checking and changing those values must occur while the relevant locks are held. A funds check performed before acquiring the lock can become stale before the subtraction, even when the subtraction itself is inside a critical section.

blocks.text: A mutex establishes both exclusion and synchronization. Unlocking and a subsequent successful lock acquisition on that mutex provide the ordering needed for protected state to become visible according to the language model. This is not merely a scheduling convention that tells threads to be polite. Bypassing the mutex because a read “usually happens later” breaks the formal basis for the access.

blocks.text: The critical section should encompass the smallest coherent state transition, not necessarily the smallest number of source lines. Splitting one invariant across several separately locked fragments can be incorrect. Conversely, holding a global lock through unrelated I/O can unnecessarily block other work. Identify the commit point where validated state changes become visible together, and keep avoidable external work outside that protected transition.

blocks.text: Returning a reference to protected data can leak the lock discipline beyond the method boundary. A getter that locks, returns a reference, and unlocks before the caller uses it does not protect the caller’s later access. Return an owned snapshot when appropriate, or expose a carefully designed operation that retains the lock through the access. Make the ownership and synchronization scope visible in the interface.

topics.title: 17.1.2 Using RAII Lock Types
topics.summary: lock_guard acquires a mutex and releases it at scope exit. unique_lock supports additional ownership operations such as deferred locking and temporary unlock, which condition variables need. scoped_lock can acquire several mutexes with a deadlock-avoidance strategy for that acquisition. These types connect lock release to ordinary and exceptional control flow.

blocks.text: Select the least flexible lock type that expresses the operation. Manual lock and unlock pairs are easy to separate accidentally with an early return or exception. RAII prevents that cleanup mistake but does not prove that the chosen critical section is large enough, that all accesses use the mutex, or that the program’s complete lock graph is acyclic.

blocks.text: RAII lock types associate lock ownership with object lifetime. lock_guard handles a simple scope. unique_lock supports deferred acquisition, unlocking, relocking, and integration with condition-variable waits. scoped_lock can acquire multiple mutexes using a deadlock-avoidance algorithm. Select the type according to the required operation rather than using the most flexible wrapper everywhere.

blocks.text: A lock object’s destructor releases only locks it owns. This makes exception paths less fragile than manual lock/unlock pairs spread across branches. It does not make the protected operation automatically exception-safe. If a mutation changes one field and then throws before restoring the invariant, releasing the mutex exposes the damaged state correctly synchronized but logically invalid. Plan mutation order and commit behavior as well as cleanup.

blocks.text: The transfer example validates amounts and destination capacity before performing its two nonthrowing arithmetic updates. Under the declared numeric bounds, the updates cannot overflow and do not allocate. Once validation succeeds while both locks are held, the commit is small and nonthrowing. This combination of locking and arithmetic reasoning is stronger than merely surrounding unsafe additions with a mutex.

blocks.text: Do not hold a lock across an arbitrary callback unless the contract explicitly permits reentrancy and blocking behavior. The callback can acquire other locks, call back into the same object, throw, or perform slow I/O. A safer architecture often gathers an owned event under the lock and invokes external behavior afterward, while acknowledging any ordering implications of that separation.

blocks.text: Moving a unique_lock transfers lock ownership, not ownership of the mutex object’s lifetime. The mutex must outlive every lock wrapper referring to it. Likewise, a locked resource that crosses an asynchronous boundary creates a long and potentially unpredictable critical section. Favor bounded synchronous state transitions when possible, and make any longer lock lifetime an explicit reviewed design choice.

topics.title: 17.2.1 Understanding Circular Wait
topics.summary: Deadlock can occur when threads each hold resources needed by the other and no one can progress. Two transfers that lock source then destination in opposite directions can create a classic circular wait. A correct individual balance update does not prevent that execution-level failure.

blocks.text: Deadlock occurs when participants cannot make progress because each waits for a resource or event that depends on another blocked participant. Circular lock acquisition is a common cause: one thread owns A and waits for B, while another owns B and waits for A. Each lock operation can be individually correct; the combined acquisition graph is not.

blocks.text: A two-object operation must handle identity as well as order. Transferring an account to itself would present the same mutex twice to a multi-lock operation. The example rejects that case before acquisition. More generally, normalize duplicate resources before applying an algorithm designed for distinct lockable objects. A data structure that aliases two logical names to one underlying owner can hide this case.

blocks.text: Deadlock is not limited to mutexes. A thread can hold a lock while waiting for a future whose producer needs that lock. A parent can wait for a child while the child waits for pipe capacity the parent is not draining. A worker pool can block every worker waiting for tasks queued to the same saturated pool. Draw wait dependencies across APIs, not only explicit lock calls.

blocks.text: A timeout may turn an indefinite wait into a reported failure, but it does not by itself repair the resource-ordering design or restore partially mutated state. If timed acquisition is part of the policy, define what the operation owns when it times out and how it releases or rolls back that state. Repeated immediate retries can create livelock even when no thread remains permanently blocked.

blocks.text: Stress tests can expose a deadlock but cannot prove its absence for all schedules. Use structural arguments: global lock order, atomic multi-lock acquisition where appropriate, no blocking callbacks under protected invariants, and explicit shutdown dependencies. Then use bounded tests and diagnostic logging to detect implementation violations of those rules.

topics.title: 17.2.2 Establishing Lock Ordering
topics.summary: A global lock order can prevent cycles when all code follows it. Alternatively, scoped_lock can acquire a known set of mutexes together using an appropriate deadlock-avoidance algorithm. Passing the same nonrecursive mutex twice is not a valid way to represent a self-transfer; handle that case before acquiring the pair.
